title: Are We Getting Heavier? The Data Behind Global Obesity

segments.label: scene 1 (title)
segments.text: Our world is physically changing, and the data shows a clear divide. In some nations, nearly half the population is now obese.

segments.label: scene 2 (world_map)
segments.text: The Bahamas leads the globe with 48.3% of its adults currently living with obesity.

segments.label: scene 3 (line)
segments.text: Yet, just a few thousand miles away, the picture is completely different. In Vietnam, that same figure sits at just 2.4%.

segments.label: scene 4 (statement)
segments.text: This massive gap highlights a modern global challenge. We are living through a period where weight trends are diverging sharply across borders.

segments.label: scene 5 (scatter)
segments.text: To understand how we arrived here, we have to look at the numbers. The reality is often more complex than individual choices.

segments.label: scene 6 (compare)
segments.text: In the United States, 41.0% of adults now face this health issue, up significantly from 27.5% at the turn of the century.

segments.label: scene 7 (multiline)
segments.text: But it isn't just one region. Whether in the United Kingdom or Australia, the trend lines are climbing toward historic highs.

segments.label: scene 8 (multiline)
segments.text: Looking at English-speaking nations, the trajectory since the turn of the millennium has been undeniably upward.

segments.label: scene 9 (compare)
segments.text: In the United Kingdom, obesity prevalence rose by 44% compared to the year 2000.

segments.label: scene 10 (counter)
segments.text: Australia has seen an even steeper climb, with rates increasing by 57% over the same period.

segments.label: scene 11 (line)
segments.text: Across the Atlantic, Canada shows a 29% increase in adult obesity rates since the start of the century.

segments.label: scene 12 (statement)
segments.text: According to Our World in Data, these nations are grappling with a complex, persistent public health shift.

segments.label: scene 13 (slope)
segments.text: When we compare the growth across these four nations, the divergence in their total figures is striking.

segments.label: scene 14 (bars)
segments.text: Ultimately, the rapid rise in obesity is a defining story of modern economic and lifestyle change.

segments.label: scene 15 (statement)
segments.text: While many nations face steady growth, some countries have diverged from the pack. The patterns we see elsewhere simply don't apply everywhere.

segments.label: scene 16 (line)
segments.text: Consider Japan. Since 2000, the share of adults with obesity has surged, reaching 5.9% in 2024.

segments.label: scene 17 (line)
segments.text: In fact, the 2024 value for Japan is 2.3 times higher than it was in 2000.

segments.label: scene 18 (line)
segments.text: Now look at Germany. After years of climbing, the trend stalled, holding steady at 20.6% since 2010.

segments.label: scene 19 (line)
segments.text: Even more unique is France. While others grew, France saw a 3% decline from 2000 to 2024.

segments.label: scene 20 (gauge)
segments.text: French rates reached their highest point of 12.9% in 2010, before trending downward.

segments.label: scene 21 (multiline)
segments.text: These contrasts show that while global pressure is real, local policies and environments play a massive role.

segments.label: scene 22 (statement)
segments.text: So, what is the engine driving these shifting numbers? One major factor is the total amount of food available to us.

segments.label: scene 23 (scatter)
segments.text: When we plot caloric availability against obesity rates across 172 countries, a clear pattern emerges.

segments.label: scene 24 (kpi)
segments.text: The data shows that these two variables generally move together, with a positive correlation of 0.24.

segments.label: scene 25 (counter)
segments.text: Take the United States. With 3,947 calories available per person per day, the obesity rate sits at 40.7%.

segments.label: scene 26 (slope)
segments.text: Other developed nations show a similar relationship between the energy provided in the food supply and weight trends.

segments.label: scene 27 (line)
segments.text: For instance, Canada has 3,590 calories available per person daily, aligning with a 25.9% obesity rate.

segments.label: scene 28 (countries_bars)
segments.text: It highlights that as caloric access rises, the prevalence of obesity often climbs in parallel, shifting public health outcomes.

segments.label: scene 29 (countries_bars)
segments.text: Let's zoom into the developed world to see how these nations compare today. While global trends are shifting, the latest 2024 data reveals a clear picture of where these countries stand.

segments.label: scene 30 (counter)
segments.text: Australia currently leads this group with an obesity rate of 30.6%. It's a significant figure that reflects a long-term upward trend.

segments.label: scene 31 (gauge)
segments.text: In the United Kingdom, 27.4% of adults are now living with obesity. It is a persistent challenge for public health officials across the nation.

segments.label: scene 32 (slope)
segments.text: Meanwhile, Canada sits at 26.0%. These three nations illustrate the heavy impact that modern, calorie-dense environments can have on population health.

segments.label: scene 33 (statement)
segments.text: But the crisis isn't confined to Western nations. Some regions are seeing even more extreme numbers.

segments.label: scene 34 (world_map)
segments.text: Egypt now reports 43.9% of its adult population living with obesity. Qatar isn't far behind, with a rate of 42.0%.

segments.label: scene 35 (race)
segments.text: These spikes in the Middle East and Africa show that the transition toward higher obesity rates is becoming a truly global phenomenon.

segments.label: scene 36 (line)
segments.text: From the U.S. at 41.0% to Belize at 43.4%, obesity is a global health challenge. These figures underscore the scale of our current reality.

segments.label: scene 37 (countries_bars)
segments.text: Yet, the story is not universal. Some regions maintain significantly lower rates, like Eritrea at 4.3%.

segments.label: scene 38 (statement)
segments.text: Data shows that local policies and environmental factors influence these outcomes. Trends are not destiny.

segments.label: scene 39 (compare)
segments.text: In the United States, we have seen a 49% surge in the share of adults with obesity since 2000.

segments.label: scene 40 (countries_bars)
segments.text: We can see where nations stand by looking at the full spectrum of global data. These patterns help us understand broader health dynamics.

segments.label: scene 41 (line)
segments.text: Looking globally, the Bahamas now leads the world with 48.3% of its adult population living with obesity.

segments.label: scene 42 (kpi)
segments.text: Thanks for watching. Please subscribe for more data-driven stories on the trends shaping our world. What do you think the data is missing? Tell us in the comments.
